subject: Vocabulary
topic: Root Words III — Latin and Greek Roots Generating Exam Vocabulary (W13 B1)

questions.explanation: B is correct. BREV (Latin brevis) = short. Abbreviate = to shorten; brevity = the quality of being brief (short); brief = short and concise. Remember: 'Brevity is the soul of wit' (Shakespeare — meaning: being concise shows intelligence). Trap: long = the opposite of brief; 'clear' = lucid (different root).

questions.stem: The root FID/FIDE (as in 'confidence', 'fidelity', 'bona fide') means:
questions.explanation: A is correct. FID/FIDE (Latin fides) = faith, trust. Confidence = con + fidence (with full faith); fidelity = faithfulness; bona fide = in good faith; fiduciary = held in trust; infidel = one without faith. Trap: fire = ignis/pyro; emotion = path/affect; knowledge = gnosis/cogn/sci.

C is correct. VER/VERI (Latin verus) = true, truth. Verify = to confirm as true; veracity = truthfulness; verdict = a true (ver) saying/declaration (dict); verity = truth; verisimilitude = appearance of being true. SSC loves this root: if you see 'ver' at the start of a word, think 'truth'. Trap: power = pot/dyn; time = chron/tempor; life = vit/viv/bio.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT share the root MORT (meaning death)?
questions.explanation: C is correct. MORBID comes from Latin morbidus = sick/diseased (morbus = disease), NOT from mort (death). Mortal = capable of dying (MORT); mortgage = pledge 'until death' (mort+gage=pledge); mortify = to cause to die with shame, or to kill/suppress (mort). Trap: students assume morbid (meaning gloomy, gruesome, relating to death) comes from 'mort' — but its root is 'morb' (disease). Morbid thinking is obsession with disease/death but the root is disease, not death.

B is correct. CRED (Latin credere) = to believe, to trust. Credible = believable; incredible = not believable; credit = trust extended (credit in business = trust to pay later); credentials = evidence of trustworthiness; credulous = too easily believing; creed = a set of beliefs. Trap: 'to grow' = cres (crescent, increase); 'to create' = creat (creation); 'to run' = curr/curs (current, cursor).

questions.stem: Words like 'benevolent', 'benefit', 'benediction', 'benefactor' all share the prefix BENE meaning:
questions.explanation: B is correct. BENE (Latin) = well, good. Benevolent = well-wishing; benefit = a good thing/advantage; benediction = good words/blessing (bene+dict=speak); benefactor = one who does good. Contrast: MALE/MALI = bad/evil (malevolent, malice). Key antonym pair: bene(good)↔male(bad) generates many SSC vocabulary words. Trap: two/double = bi (bicycle); around = peri/circum; below = sub/under.

C is correct. GREG (Latin grex/gregis) = flock, herd, group. Congregate = to gather as a flock (con+greg); gregarious = preferring to be in a group; segregate = to separate from the group (se=apart); egregious = literally 'standing out from the flock' (e=out), now meaning outstandingly bad. Trap: step/walk = ambul/grad/gress (ambulance, graduation); speak = dict/log; rule = arch/crac (monarchy, democracy).

B is correct. CLAM/CLAIM (Latin clamare) = to cry out, to shout. Exclaim = to cry out in surprise; proclamation = public crying out/announcement (pro=forth); clamour = loud confused noise; disclaim = to cry out against/deny; reclaim = to cry out again/recover. Trap: 'to hide' = occult/cel (conceal); 'to climb' = similar sound but different root (scale/ascend); 'to claim ownership' = a secondary meaning derived from the 'asserting' sense of clamare, but the primary root meaning is 'to cry out'.

questions.stem: Choose the word from the PATHOS/PATH root (meaning feeling, suffering) that fits: 'His speech was full of ___ that moved the audience to tears.'
questions.explanation: D is correct. PATHOS = quality that evokes pity, sadness or deep feeling in an audience (from Greek pathos = feeling/suffering). A speech 'full of pathos' that 'moved the audience to tears' = speech that evoked deep emotional feeling. Trap: apathy = absence of feeling (a+path=without feeling — the opposite); empathy = feeling INTO another's experience (em+path); sympathy = feeling TOGETHER with someone (sym+path = alongside). The exact word for 'evoking pity/emotion in a speech or artistic work' = pathos.

questions.stem: The root PEND/PENS (as in 'depend', 'suspend', 'appendix', 'compensate') primarily means:
questions.explanation: B is correct. PEND/PENS (Latin pendere) = to hang, to weigh. Depend = to hang from (de+pend = hang from); suspend = to hang from above (sus=sub+pend); appendix = something hung onto (ap+pend+ix); compensate = to weigh against/counterbalance; pendant = something hanging; pendulum = hanging weight; impending = hanging over (about to happen). Trap: write = script/graph; push/drive = puls/pel (impel, pulse); breathe = spir (respiratory, inspire).
